body:
In May this year, research by IPE Real Assets showed that the aggregate assets of the top 150 real estate investors – comprising institutional asset owners such as pension, insurance and sovereign wealth funds – had returned to growth after declining in 2025, reaching $2.18trn (€1.98trn).

This month, it was the turn of real estate investment managers. The good news persisted: growth in assets under management (AUM) returned to positive territory as well, rising from €5.72trn to €5.94trn. This industry had suffered a longer decline dating back to 2022.

The findings are consistent with numbers from real estate associations ANREV, INREV and NCREIF, which reported in June that global AUM had risen 5.7% to €3.8trn – the first increase since 2021.

However, these big headline figures, which show an asset class back in (albeit moderate) expansion mode, come at a time when real estate is still feeling the pressure. The recent rise in government bond yields and the return of interest-rate increases is piling further pressure on an asset class that has yet to fully recover from its recent downturn.

Long road to recovery?

Last week, PwC and the Urban Land Institute’s annual Emerging Trends in Real Estate report for Europe suggested that the asset class was set for more stagnation. “Europe’s property industry faces a longer-than-anticipated recovery, as higher bond yields, prolonged geopolitical instability and questions over real estate’s appeal against other asset classes continue to weigh on sentiment,” it said.

On the other hand, fundamentals of real estate are strong, with steady profitability and resilient occupier demand, it added. There are also signs that institutional investors could begin allocating more capital to real estate after becoming fully or over-exposed to the asset class in recent years. Hodes Weill has just published its latest annual survey of real estate investors, which found that the gap between investors’ target allocations and their actual exposure is at its greatest since 2022.

Institutional target allocations to real estate held steady at 10.7% this year, after declining last year, according to the 14th annual Institutional Real Estate Allocations Monitor, published by Hodes Weill (now part of Chatham Financial Company), and Cornell University’s Baker Program in Real Estate. Investors expect to increase target allocations by 10 basis points to 10.8% in 2027, with 22% of institutions planning to raise targets over the next 12 months – the highest share since 2022.

Furthermore, approximately 54% of institutions report being under-allocated, up from 40% in 2025, representing the highest reported under-allocation since 2021. The report authors have applied this to an estimated US$147trn of global institutional AUM and concluded that it implies approximately US$1.8trn of potential incremental real estate investment.

“Institutions have held their target allocations steady through a period that tested confidence, as renewed interest rate volatility and geopolitical uncertainty delayed the recovery many investors anticipated coming into the year,” said Douglas Weill, senior managing director at Hodes Weill. “The widening gap between actual and target allocations reflects strong public equity performance and implies meaningful capacity for new investment. While institutions remain cautious, many are positioning to invest selectively at reset valuations, and as distributions recover, this allocation headroom could support a renewed pace of investment.”

Both the PwC/ULI and Hodes Weill reports observed marked asset-allocation competition from infrastructure. Hodes Weill found that, for the first time, infrastructure ranked as the leading asset class competing with real estate for allocations, named by 60% of institutions, followed by private credit (54%), fixed income (48%) and private equity (44%). According to PwC/ULI, the main factor holding back allocations to real estate is its relative value versus other asset classes, with one in three respondents naming infrastructure as the asset class generating the greatest competition.

This month’s most-read article this month concerned the largest US public pension plan approving $2.7bn of commitments to real assets investments, of which $1.7bn went to infrastructure and $1bn to real estate. If it is possible to treat California Public Employees’ Retirement System (CalPERS) as a proxy of sorts for US pension fund capital the news suggests appetite for both real estate and infrastructure. Half of the $1bn went to a pan-European student housing fund managed by Global Student Accommodation, and the remaining $500m to US value-add/opportunistic residential fund manager by Greystar.

Meanwhile, Teacher Retirement System (TRS) of Texas – another very large US public pension fund – has committed $1bn to real estate across five strategies, including a $500m allocation to the IDR Strategic Opportunities Fund, which provides access to core and core-plus open-ended funds in the US. It also invested in infrastructure, but at a relatively smaller volume, committing a total at $275m to three funds.

Questions remain over the outlook for real estate, while rising interest rates and competition from other asset classes will provide ongoing pressure. But allocations for real estate are there and there is potential for more institutional capital to open up for the asset class going into 2027.
